name: dang-187
title: Make nullable GraphQL object fields actually nullable
head: 4e4300aec1216ffe45b82a45aebcb98a13d7d226
notes: Known issues compiled from two reviews of the PR at 4e4300a: reviewer v1 at STANDARD depth, and a plain 'adversarial review <pr url>' session. 'confirmed' means a reviewer reproduced it with a test; 'claimed' means it was argued from the code but not reproduced. Labels are unvetted until the PR author confirms them: 'vetted' is null until the author marks an issue 'real' or 'dismiss' (in vetting.md, which overrides a null here).

issues.summary: A probed nullable interface/union handle is swapped for one whose chain ends in an inline fragment on the concrete type, but its static type stays the interface. Multi-type inline fragments on it get nested under the concrete fragment and fail GraphQL validation ('Fragment cannot be spread here...'); a single non-matching fragment now errors instead of returning null. Also narrowTo in resolveObject's no-loader path, and `n: Node` parameters fed a probed value.

After a nullable object is probed and reloaded through node(id:), GraphQLError.path reports ["node", ...] instead of the original field path: `user(id:"User:2").manager.alwaysFails` gives ["user","manager","alwaysFails"], but binding the manager with let first gives ["node","alwaysFails"]. Whether a value went through a let changes the error path, undercutting errors.md's advice to inspect e.path.

The handle bound by a `case` type arm no longer equals the value it matched: with `let f = favoriteNode`, `case (f) { p: Post => p == f }` is false, because equality compares QueryChain pointers and resolveObject builds a new node(id:) chain. Before the PR the binding was the operand itself.

Loading through node(id:) assumes the server can load every type that implements node's return type (nodeCanReturn checks only that). Some Relay servers load only a subset, or apply different permissions than the original path. When node returns null, later non-null leaves fail with 'null is not allowed for String', far from the cause, where before the PR the original chain worked. The test server was rewritten to globally unique 'User:1' IDs to fit the assumption. Suggested: fall back to the original chain, or make load-by-ID opt-in for non-Dagger schemas.

The 'no error means the parent was null' rule has an exception: querybuilder.unpack steps over inline fragments, so a non-null leaf under a non-matching fragment comes back nil with no error. Safe today because every fragment on a MaybeNull chain follows a __typename check, but the soundness argument in GraphQLFunction.Call doesn't mention fragments, and a stale or wrong __typename would silently become null.

isNullableObjectType excludes lists, so a nullable [User] field on an ordinary chain never compares == null, yet `user(id:"User:1").manager.posts.posts == null` is true because the list inherits MaybeNull. Whether a nullable list can be null depends on the path used to reach it.

nodeCanReturn accepts any interface or union type unconditionally. When knowsType fails (the concrete type isn't in scope), resolveObject loads with the abstract g.TypeName, which can produce node(id:){... on SomeUnion} and fail GraphQL validation if the union doesn't overlap node's return type.

selectedThrough is written onto AST nodes during Infer and never reset, so runtime correctness depends on inference having run on that exact node. Harmless while nodes aren't shared between positions or inferred concurrently; a node synthesized at eval time without the flag gets an extra (safe) probe, and nothing enforces the opposite case.

The PR goes further than the Dagger Go SDK, which probes only nullable fields, fetches only id, and keeps the declared interface type. This PR also probes non-null fields selected off an unprobed nullable field, handles unions, and narrows to the concrete type (an extra query in `case` on non-null abstract types). Reasonable, but 'matches the Dagger SDKs' overstates it.

Unneeded queries: SelectField("id") re-fetches an id the handle already has in KnownID (seen in the 'probes argument expressions' test); resolveObject re-fetches id for handles with KnownID such as @expectedType loads; the list check selects __typename on every element just to learn whether the list is null.
In needsConcreteType, `g.MaybeNull ||` is never true: a MaybeNull handle only escapes unprobed on a mutation chain, which returns early on g.IsMutation. The accompanying comment is misleading.

interop.md's 'Laziness' paragraph still says no request is sent until a value is forced, contradicting the new 'Nullable object fields' section right below it, which describes probes on let, argument passing, comparison, etc.

The agent skill reference still says no request is sent until a GraphQL value is forced; the PR now probes nullable object/interface/union fields when they escape the chain, and `case` with concrete patterns on abstract handles sends a query.

The agent skill reference still says mutations follow the same laziness rules as queries; the PR makes nullable object fields reached through a mutation never null-probed and stops `case` resolving concrete types there. interop.md was updated; this copy wasn't.

The agent skill reference lists only leaf fields and .{{ }} selections as GraphQL execution points; the PR adds a third (a possibly-null handle escaping the chain is probed), and rescue classification now treats it as a leaf. errors.md was updated; this twin wasn't.

The rescue analysis update misses nullable root fields reached through the schema's module name: `Test.maybeUser(id: "User:1") rescue null` still warns that a lazy value leaves the rescue without executing, though at runtime it is probed inside the rescue; the unqualified form doesn't warn. classifyGQLSelect and selectMayBeNull don't treat the import-module receiver as a root. Found by reviewer v4 run 2.

A `case` over a union returned by a mutation, with one type pattern per member and no `else`, still type-checks as exhaustive, but the change never resolves an abstract handle on a mutation chain (`if g.IsMutation || !g.isAbstract() { return false }`: asking for its type would re-send the mutation). At runtime no arm matches and the program fails with the internal "exhaustive case did not match the value" error, which the code describes as a compiler bug. The new docs say such values match only interface patterns or `else`, which a union has no interface pattern for. Result unions (`User | ValidationError`) are a common mutation return type. Suggested fixes: treat a mutation-rooted abstract operand as non-exhaustive at inference (require `else`), or raise a clear error in Case.Eval pointing to `.{{... on A}}`. Found by reviewer v5 runs 1-3 (all three; reproduced with a probe schema in run 1); run 1 showed it only as a one-line overflow concern.

A non-null lazy inline fragment `... on User!` on a null receiver now evaluates to null instead of raising the type-assertion error, though the result is still typed `User!`: `let u = node(id: "nope").{{... on User!}}` binds null and `u.name == null` holds for a `String!`, and the null only fails later at some typed boundary ("null is not allowed for Test.User!"). At the merge base the unprobed handle's empty __typename made matchLazyInlineFragment raise. The change's own test (test_graphql_nullable_object.dang:109) asserts the null. Suggested fix: in evalGraphQLLazyInlineFragments (and the list variant, and ObjectSelection.Eval's null-receiver early return), raise the assertion error when the receiver is null and any fragment is NonNull, or infer the result nullable when the receiver is. Found by reviewer v5 runs 2 and 3 (a voter reproduced it in run 3).

sound.summary: convertGraphQLResultToModule returning null for a nil result is correct, and probing only when a value leaves the chain holds up.
Static rescue classification matches runtime behaviour, including (x ?? y).f and x!.f. The qualified Module.field form is excluded: that gap is the issue qualified-root-rescue.
Union probes use per-member `... on T { id }` fragments selecting ids of one shared type, avoiding GraphQL field-merge conflicts.
No mutation is sent twice; the mutation test enforces it.
An argument evaluated inside a chain that is being selected through is still probed.
